raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old female from Yala Province, Southern Thailand, presented with high-grade fever during a vacation in Bangkok. She developed fever, polyarthralgia, and polymyalgia for 5 days; generalized erythematous rash was noted 1 day preadmission. She had no known underlying or familial disease, and no history of hair loss, oral ulcer, or photosensitivity. She denied traveling, or exposure to cattle, flooding, goat dairy products, unusual foods, or pets. Physical examination on admission showed temperature 38.6 C, BP 105/60 mmHg, PR 98/min, RR 24/min, mildly dehydrated lips, bilateral injected conjunctivae, bilateral palpable cervical lymph nodes ~0.5-1 cm in diameter, with predominant tenderness on the left postauricular nodes, and pain in the calves and joints of the extremities. Normal cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurological findings were noted. Only a just-palpable, soft liver was noted on abdominal examination. CBC on admission (D0) is shown in Table 1. Her symptoms were alleviated by analgesics (for pain) and paracetamol (antipyretic). She was presumptively diagnosed with leptospirosis and began treatment with 2 gm/day of ceftriaxone.
However, more aggravated joint and muscle pain, with particular digital swellings at both hands and feet, were reported the following day. Physical examination supported this clinically, with puffy hands and feet with marked tenderness at the bilateral knuckles, including the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP and PIP) joints, and proximal muscle weakness in both upper and lower extremities. CBC and blood chemistry analysis the following day (D2) are shown in Table 1. Urine analysis found a yellow, clear fluid, specific gravity 1.020, pH 6.5, protein 0.0075 g/L, glucose negative, WBC 0-1/HPF, RBC 3-5/HPF, and epithelium 0-1/HPF. There was no evidence of hemolysis proven by direct microscopic blood film slide and Coomb's test negative. Serological tests were conducted for possible infections, including chikungunya disease. The IgM rapid chikungunya test and IgG using HAI both showed negative. IFA tests for scrub typhus and murine typhus showed negative for IgM and IgG. IFA tests for leptospiral antibody IgM and IgG were negative. However, serology for dengue infection and lyme disease were not tested because of not compatible clinical feature and endemicity of the diseases.
Three days later, the patient looked edematous and an erythematous rash had spread throughout her body. Physical examination revealed progressive painful joints and digits. She had to stay in bed because she was unable to get up from a prone position. CBC and blood chemistry results on day 5 are shown in Table 1. Elevated muscle enzyme was detected. ESR was 83 mm/hr. Urine analysis found a yellow clear fluid with specific gravity 1.015, pH 6.0, protein 0.0025 g/L, glucose negative, WBC 1-2/HPF, RBC 1-2/HPF, and epithelium 0-1/HPF. Hemocultures of 3 specimens showed negative. Secondary causes of polymyositis were assessed. Anti-HIV antibody was negative. Intravenous ceftriaxone was discontinued. High-dose steroid treatment was initiated to control inflammation, with 20 mg/day of dexamethasone, which was switched to 0.8 mg/kg/D oral prednisolone. After 3-5 days of steroid treatment, a significant clinical response was noted. She became afebrile, reported reduced pain in the joints, and resumed normal life after 1 week of treatment. CBC and blood chemistry results on D10 are shown in Table 1. ESR was 64 mm/hr. 
Serological testing confirmed acute chikungunya infection by EIA IgM 338 Units, IgG 15 Units. Serological tests were run each week, after the rapid tests. Other immunological laboratory investigations showed antinuclear antibody positive 1 : 320, speckled typed, anti-dsDNA negative, anti-SM negative, anti-JO-1 negative, VDRL nonreactive, and rheumatoid factor negative. Four to six weeks later, the patient improved markedly and resumed her normal activities. Steroid dosage was tapered off 10-15 mg/d every 2 weeks, and discontinued at 10 weeks. Antinuclear antibody levels were tested repeatedly and became negative 3 months after the onset of illness. The patient is now doing well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old female presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, polyarthralgia, and polymyalgia, and a 1-day history of generalized erythematous rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, from Yala Province in Southern Thailand, developed high-grade fever, polyarthralgia, and polymyalgia for 5 days while vacationing in Bangkok, with a generalized erythematous rash appearing 1 day before admission. On hospital day 2, she experienced worsening joint and muscle pain with digital swelling of both hands and feet. By day 5, her rash had spread generalized across her body, facial/limb edema worsened, and severe joint pain and proximal muscle weakness rendered her bedbound and unable to rise from a prone position.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known underlying or familial disease. Resident of Yala Province, Southern Thailand, on vacation in Bangkok. Denied other travel or exposure to cattle, flooding, goat dairy products, unusual foods, or pets.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, polyarthralgia, polymyalgia, generalized rash, digital swelling, and proximal muscle weakness; negative for alopecia (hair loss), oral ulcers, or photosensitivity.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: temperature 38.6 C, blood pressure 105/60 mm Hg, pulse rate 98/min, respiratory rate 24/min. Mildly dehydrated lips, bilateral injected conjunctivae, and bilateral palpable cervical lymph nodes (~0.5-1 cm in diameter) with predominant tenderness over the left postauricular nodes. Tenderness in the calves and extremity joints. Abdominal exam showed a just-palpable, soft liver; cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurological exams were normal. On hospital day 2: puffy hands and feet with marked tenderness of bilateral knuckles (MCP, PIP, and DIP joints) and proximal muscle weakness in both upper and lower extremities. On hospital day 5: generalized edema, widespread erythematous rash, progressive painful joints and digits, and inability to rise from a prone position.
objective.routine_investigations: Urinalysis (day 2): yellow, clear, specific gravity 1.020, pH 6.5, protein 0.0075 g/L, glucose negative, WBC 0-1/HPF, RBC 3-5/HPF, epithelium 0-1/HPF. Direct microscopic blood film and Coombs test: negative for hemolysis. Rapid chikungunya IgM and HAI IgG (initial): negative. Indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) for scrub typhus, murine typhus, and leptospirosis (IgM and IgG): negative. Day 5 labs: elevated muscle enzymes, ESR 83 mm/hr; repeat urinalysis showed yellow clear fluid, specific gravity 1.015, pH 6.0, protein 0.0025 g/L, glucose negative, WBC 1-2/HPF, RBC 1-2/HPF, epithelium 0-1/HPF. Blood cultures (3 specimens): negative. Anti-HIV antibody: negative. VDRL: nonreactive. Day 10 ESR: 64 mm/hr.
objective.advanced_workup: Autoimmune panel: antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive at 1:320 (speckled pattern), anti-dsDNA negative, anti-Sm negative, anti-Jo-1 negative, and rheumatoid factor (RF) negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute chikungunya virus infection complicated by secondary polymyositis, polyarthritis, and transient ANA positivity. Initial presumptive diagnosis of leptospirosis was excluded by negative leptospiral IFA and negative blood cultures; scrub typhus, murine typhus, HIV, syphilis, and SLE/autoimmune myositis were also ruled out. Confirmation: Weekly follow-up enzyme immunoassay (EIA) confirmed acute chikungunya infection with CHIKV IgM 338 Units and IgG 15 Units. Management and outcome: Initially treated with analgesics, paracetamol, and empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g/day (discontinued on day 5). Initiated on high-dose corticosteroids (IV dexamethasone 20 mg/day, then transitioned to oral prednisolone 0.8 mg/kg/day) to control myositis and joint inflammation. She became afebrile with marked pain reduction within 3-5 days, resumed normal activities after 1 week, and tapered off steroids completely over 10 weeks (10-15 mg/day reduction every 2 weeks). Repeat ANA testing became negative at 3 months post-onset, and she recovered completely.
